I used to run a BBS on my old Amiga 500 (later Amiga 1200), using Xenolink. It was a lot of fun. Toward the end of my interest I had the bright idea to develop terminal software that recognised ASCII codes and actually did simple graphics on the local computer, like boxes, circles and paint operations. Then the WWW happened.

I remember when my brother got a screaming 2400 baud modem for our 386 with a 40 mhz turbo button. I used BBS's mostly for downloading Calvin and Hobbes pictures IIRC. I had a few floppies full of them. I should dig those up sometime and look at what I thought was important back then.

Used an Atari 800XL and a 14.4 modem in the mid-80s to connect to BBS systems. It all came to a screeching halt when my mother received a $500 telephone bill one month. When I went off to college I then became a point in the Fidonet system. Great times.

I ran C-NET 9.6, and then C-NEt 10.0. You could mod the hell out of those. The core was written in basic with the communications and some disk crap written in ML. The only reason I think they were written in ML was to introduce some copy protection, that was cracked (according to the author in a post in an 80's BBS forum) in an astonishing short time.

It started with a c64, 1541, and a totaltel 300 baud modem. Eventually I upgraded to 2 SFD's (1 meg parallel drives that were blazing fast, faster than the IBM 5.25's ever managed), and a 1670 1200 baud modem. And then later to a 286 in the 90s. The BBS pretty much shut its doors in 1995 running on that 286.

I'm still friends with a few people from those days. Friends as in play with their kids and cook out with. And nearly all my life has been shaped by those days. I got my first IT jobs because people knew me in the scene.

The BBS documentary is ok... but each area code has its own story to tell. It's own cast of characters.

Here I am on a local 90s radio show with one of my friends (who I still talk to):

http://iama.stupid.cow.org/Audio/31337-1.mp3

http://iama.stupid.cow.org/Audio/31337-3.mp3

and me reading the Hacker's Manifesto. I used to read this at every 2600 meeting to start the meetings. http://iama.stupid.cow.org/Audio/HACKER3.WAV http://iama.stupid.cow.org/Audio/Hacker4.wav

Paying for access... Yeah. That always meant being a lamer to me. Using real names? No. I was on various boards others had to pay for or use their real names just because I was krad. I had a statement on my BBS that if you liked it and wanted to donate money to take the money to the animal shelter or food kitchen. Why should my users pay for my hobby?

We had some serious parties. Lots of alcohol, weed, sex, and of course conversations and trading of warez. Our Halloween parties were awesome. Beach parties too. The idea of the geek or the nerd that didnt fit in? That wasnt my experience. We were the cool kids. The so called cool kids not in the scene? Sleeper, cattle, sheep, the herd, status quo, dweeb and lamers who didnt have anything to say that was worth listening to. Women not into computers? In what world? There were some fucken super stunning and beautiful 'modem chicks' in my area in the day. And they were smart. Some programmed. Some created shit in Koala Paint or played with SIDS. One of them gave me my starting knowledge in UNIX. I'm still friends with some of them.

Doors... Murder Motel, and some of its clones, were the fucken best. I got lucky... It started on the C64 as a c-net subprogram (there was an area in the basic code filled with line numbers an :'s. Code would be loaded into this area for featured areas such as files area, msgs, email, and so on) and then was converted to the PC. I ran my BBS for 10 years...

What I feel for all of that... Kids now may feel for what they have... But we were special. If you heard keywords in public you know they were a BBSER...

I road public transportation to high skewl. One day I am riding the bus and over hear a conversation.. After a bit I interject. "Yer trinity, are you?" a shock and a nod. "And you are Gumshoe Grant?" Yeah, now who the hell are you? "No on one."... Now everyone uses those key words.

When talking of tying onions to one's belt and bumble bees on nickles one rambles... Sorry. I was in 1985. I'm back now.

I am mentioned in 2 text files on textfiles.com... and am in the BBS list...

Does anyone recall the horse shit with the 38400 standards? None of them were ever 38400 if I recall. They all used compression in order to get that. I recall testing it with zips and getting less than 9600 baud. There were two standards, I think one was HST, I dont recall the other. You could buy a dual standard modem too...

One of the BBS's in my area became an ISP... I loved free dial up and shell accounts...

Someone in my area code wrote a C-NET 10.0 clone for the ADAM computer. I still wish I could meet that kid.

Just as I came onto the scene the group known as 2300 club folded. Not the 2600 club. The history from that era appears so lost. The rumors include cars being blown up and lots of acid being had.

Crazy what one can find on the internet...
